title: Fault-tolerant and fully addressable unitary logical gates via round-robin sparsification
abstract: For quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes, the ability to manipulate individual logical units of information, i.e. the use of addressable gates, enables maximal utility of their efficient encoding. We introduce explicit low-depth unitary circuits that realize fully addressable and fault-tolerant two-qubit Clifford gates for a subset of two-dimensional translationally invariant qLDPC codes. Our transversal unitaries are created by applying a geometrically structured sparsification procedure to round-robin circuits. We verify the general applicability of our protocol by proposing and numerically simulating a range of addressable CZs between toric, cyclic hypergraph-product, color, gross, and directional codes, demonstrating fault-tolerant memory-like logical error rate scaling.
summary: This paper develops a novel technique to create fault-tolerant and fully addressable two-qubit gates for various qLDPC quantum error-correcting codes. By applying a structured sparsification procedure to initial round-robin circuits, the authors significantly reduce gate depth while maintaining fault tolerance. This work is vital for realizing scalable quantum computation using lattice-based error correction.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of creating fault-tolerant and fully addressable unitary logical gates for quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes.
main_result: The authors introduce a sparsification procedure applied to round-robin circuits that successfully realizes low-depth, fault-tolerant, and addressable two-qubit Clifford gates for a wide class of 2DTI qLDPC codes.
method: The core method involves applying a geometrically structured sparsification procedure, utilizing stabilizer deformations and the cylinder trick, to reduce the depth of initial round-robin logical circuits.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum error correction (QEC) codes, specifically two-dimensional translationally invariant (2DTI) qLDPC codes, including the toric, color, and various hypergraph-product codes.
key_observables: Logical error rate (LER), gate depth (aiming for constant depth like 3), and fault-tolerance scaling with physical error rate.
important_parameters: The fault distance ($d$) of the code, the physical error rate ($p$), and the code structure (e.g., lattice type, boundary conditions).
main_assumptions: The initial round-robin circuits are not naturally fault-tolerant, necessitating the sparsification procedure; the generalization to CX gates is stated as trivial for CSS codes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the sparsification process on the toric code, showing logical operators and circuit steps. Other figures benchmark LER scaling for various codes and compare tCZ gates against code surgery operations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the sparsification technique using stabilizer deformations and the cylinder trick, verifies the protocol on several 2DTI codes, and concludes with numerical simulations comparing the resulting gate performance against alternative methods like code surgery.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract QEC codes, the techniques for achieving low-depth, fault-tolerant gates are crucial for scaling up any quantum computation platform, including those based on AMO systems.

(a) The vertical and horizontal Z-logical operators of the two logical qubits of a distance d = 3 toric code with qubits on edges (dashed lines are identified with the opposite edges). On the lower right, we show a Z-stabilizer. (b) Multiple representatives of the vertical Z-logical operator. (c) An RR logical CZ circuit, with individual CZ gates shown by colored lines. (d) A stabilizer deformation, with the stabilizer highlighted, equivalent to a logical identity. (e) The sparsification procedure, consisting of conjugation of the circuit in (c) with various highlighted stabilizer deformations....

FIG. 2. Propagation of faults through a toric tCZ. (a) Error propagation rules through a CZ gate. (b) X errors propagate to Zs in two distinct ways: (i) Weight 3 but anti- aligned with least-weight logicals, which natively preserves the distance, or (ii) Weight-2 along a logical. The original X error creates additional detection events which can identify this mechanism without reducing distance.

FIG. 3. Using the cylinder trick to extract disjoint logical representatives for RR sparsification on 2DTI codes. (a) Defining lattice elements: (i) edges support h and v qubits (purple); X (red) and Z (blue) ancillae are on vertices • and plaquettes □respectively. (ii) Monomials denote cardinal translations across the lattice. (iii) Stabilizers can be defined via polynomials, shown for cHGP2. (b) Z-Symmetries of 2DTI codes are sets of checks that always product to identity: Any X error leaves an even parity of syndromes in the support of the cHGP2 symmetry. FIG. 4. L for more 2DTI codes. We show the maximum disjoint logical representative set L of size |J| obtained from the sliding cylinder trick for the (a) d = 6 color and (b) d = 4 cHGP3 codes. Similar to Fig. 3, adjacent disjoint logical representatives are shown via bright and dark blue highlights on the symmetry that supports them. For cHGP3, |J| < d.

FIG. 5. Inter-code addressable tCZs with Cα = Cβ. We show logical error rate scaling with physical error rate for a transversal Cα0Zβ0 (blue) compared to memory (orange) across code distances. Across panels, Cα is respectively defined to be toric (left), cyclic HGP-2 (center), or color and NE3N directional (right) codes. In all plots, tCZ scaling matches that of memory. In the center panel, we further change the logical operator targeted in Cβ via the tCZ to other vertical (red) and horizontal (red) Z logical operators, showing unchanged logical performance.
